text: Tomato_Bacterial_Spot is caused by Xanthomonas perforans / vesicatoria. Common names: Tomato Bacterial Spot (en), ٹماٹر کا بیکٹیریائی دھبہ (ur), د ټماټرو باکتریایي ټاپي (ps). Severe foliar and fruit disease in warm, wet climates.
Small, dark brown, water-soaked spots on leaves, stems, and fruits. Lesions turn dark brown to black with yellow halos. Fruit lesions appear as raised scab-like spots, diminishing fruit quality.
Favored by high temperatures (24–30°C), splashing rain, overhead irrigation, and dew. Bacteria enter through stomata or mechanical wounds and survive on seed or crop debris.
Use disease-free certified seeds. Avoid overhead irrigation; apply drip or furrow watering. Practice a 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops and disinfect stakes and equipment.
Apply foliar bio-fungicides containing Bacillus subtilis or Pseudomonas fluorescens at early disease onset to suppress bacterial populations.
Apply Copper Hydroxide mixed with Mancozeb (protectant bactericide combination). Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Sanitize tools, clear solanaceous weeds (nightshades), stake plants for improved airflow, and avoid field work when foliage is wet.
Wear chemical-resistant gloves, protective coveralls, and respiratory protection during copper-mancozeb spraying operations.

Tomato_Early_Blight is caused by Alternaria solani. Common names: Tomato Early Blight (en), ٹماٹر کا اگیتا جھلساؤ (ur), د ټماټرو دمخه سوځیدنه (ps). Common foliar disease affecting solanaceous crops in humid conditions.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Dark brown circular spots with characteristic concentric rings ('target-board' pattern) surrounded by yellow chlorotic halos. Older lower leaves affected first, progressing upward.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Favored by warm temperatures (24–29°C) and high humidity or frequent dew. Spores travel by wind, rain splash, and tools. Overwinters in infected crop debris.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Practice 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops. Prune lower leaves up to 30 cm from ground to prevent soil splash. Use drip irrigation and straw mulching.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Foliar application of Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide. Apply Neem seed kernel extract (5%) as a bio-rational.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Apply contact protectant Mancozeb or systemic Difenoconazole/Azoxystrobin. Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Use certified seed, stake plants for ventilation, clear nightshade weeds, and avoid overhead watering.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Wear protective gloves, eye goggles, and coveralls during spraying operations.

text: Tomato_Fusarium_Wilt is caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici. Common names: Fusarium Wilt (en), ٹماٹر کی فوساریئم مرجھاؤ (ur), د ټماټرو فیوزاریوم مړاوی (ps). Soil-borne vascular wilt pathogen.
Yellowing and wilting starting on lower leaves, often restricted to one side of the branch or plant ('one-sided yellowing'). Vascular discoloration inside the lower stem turns reddish-brown.
Favored by warm soil temperatures (27–28°C) and acidic sandy soils. The fungal pathogen persists indefinitely in soil as chlamydospores and enters via roots.
Plant resistant tomato cultivars (bearing F1/F2 resistance genes). Maintain soil pH between 6.5 and 7.0 using agricultural lime. Rotate crops for 5+ years with non-hosts.
Incorporate Trichoderma viride or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens into soil at transplanting to colonize root zones.
Soil drench with Carbendazim or Thiophanate-methyl at seedling stage. Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Soil solarization during summer months, use resistant rootstocks/varieties, and prevent movement of infested soil across fields.
Avoid inhaling dust during lime or bio-rational application; wear protective gloves and respirator.
Tomato_Healthy represents healthy Solanum lycopersicum foliage. Common names: Healthy Tomato (en), صحت مند ٹماٹر (ur), روغ ټماټر (ps). Free from foliar pathogens or nutrient deficiencies.
Leaves exhibit uniform dark green coloration, turgid structure, and clean blade margins with no necrotic or chlorotic spots, wilting, or pest damage.
Maintained under balanced soil moisture, proper solar radiation, ambient temperature (20–28°C), and adequate plant nutrition (N-P-K + micronutrients).
Maintain routine balanced fertigation (N-P-K), scheduled drip irrigation, staking/trellising, and regular weed management.
Preventive soil inoculation with mycorrhizal fungi or Trichoderma spp. to enhance root nutrient uptake and systemic resilience.
No synthetic chemical intervention required. Apply micronutrient foliar spray (Zinc/Boron) if soil test indicates deficiency.
Regular field scouting, crop rotation, sanitation of farm equipment, and balanced irrigation management.
Follow standard agricultural hygiene and safe handling practices when applying organic fertilizers.
Tomato_Late_Blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans. Common names: Tomato Late Blight (en), ٹماٹر کا پچھیتا جھلساؤ (ur), د ټماټرو وروسته سوځیدنه (ps). Extremely destructive oomycete pathogen.

Large, irregular water-soaked pale green to dark brown oily lesions on leaves. White cottony growth appears on underside of leaves under high humidity. Dark greasy stem lesions and brown leathery rot on fruit.
Favored by cool, wet weather (15–22°C) with relative humidity > 90%. Windborne sporangia spread rapidly over long distances.
Destroy volunteer tomato/potato plants and infected crop residues. Space plants for maximum air circulation. Avoid overhead irrigation.
Apply copper octanoate or bio-control agents such as Bacillus subtilis preventively prior to wet cool weather events.
Apply systemic oomyceticides (Metalaxyl-M + Mancozeb, Dimethomorph, or Cymoxanil). Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Plant resistant cultivars, monitor weather forecasts for late blight warnings, and maintain strict field hygiene.
Wear chemical-resistant suit, neoprene gloves, and full face-shield when handling systemic oomyceticides.

Tomato_Leaf_Mold is caused by Passalora fulva (syn. Fulvia fulva). Common names: Tomato Leaf Mold (en), ٹماٹر کے پتے کا پھپھوند (ur), د ټماټرو د پاڼو مولډ (ps). Common greenhouse and high-tunnel disease.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Pale green to yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces corresponding to olive-green to dark brown velvety mold on lower leaf surfaces. Older leaves wither and die.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Favored by high relative humidity (> 85%) and moderate temperatures (20–24°C). Common in poorly ventilated greenhouses or dense canopies.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Increase greenhouse ventilation, reduce humidity using exhaust fans, space plants generously, and prune lower leaves to promote airflow.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Apply foliar sprays of Trichoderma harzianum or bio-rational potassium bicarbonate to inhibit spore germination.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Apply protective fungicides such as Chlorothalonil or Difenoconazole at initial symptom detection. Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Grow leaf mold-resistant varieties (carrying Cf resistance genes), manage indoor humidity, and avoid wetting foliage during irrigation.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Wear respiratory protection, eye protection, and protective clothing during greenhouse spraying.

text: Tomato_Miner is caused by leafminer larvae (Liriomyza spp.). Common names: Tomato Leafminer (en), ٹماٹر کا پتا سرنگ گر (ur), د ټماټرو د پاڼو مائنر (ps). Insect pest feeding inside leaf mesophyll.
Winding, whitish or translucent serpentine mines/tunnels visible inside leaf blades. Severe mining reduces photosynthetic leaf area and causes premature leaf desiccation.
Adult flies puncture leaves to feed and lay eggs. Larvae hatch and feed internally inside mesophyll layer. Favored by warm dry weather.
Install yellow sticky traps (30–40 traps/hectare) to monitor and catch adult flies. Remove heavily mined lower leaves and weeds.
Conserve or release parasitic wasps (Diglyphus isaea or Dacnusa sibirica). Apply Neem oil (Azadirachtin 1%) foliar sprays.

Apply translaminar insecticides such as Abamectin or Cyromazine. Note: Active ingredients only. Fungicides are ineffective against leafminers. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Use insect-proof mesh in greenhouses, maintain weed-free buffer zones, and rotate insecticides to prevent resistance.
Wear protective gloves, respirator mask, and chemical coveralls during translaminar insecticide applications.

Tomato_Mosaic_Virus is caused by Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV). Common names: Tomato Mosaic Virus (en), ٹماٹر کا موزیک وائرس (ur), د ټماټرو موزیک وائرس (ps). Highly stable mechanically transmitted tobamovirus.
Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves, blistered or fern-like leaf distortion (shoestring symptom), plant stunting, and internal brown necrosis in fruits.
Mechanically transmitted via contaminated hands, tools, clothing, and seed coat. Highly persistent in crop residues and soil for extended periods.
Wash hands with soap or 20% non-fat dry milk solution before handling plants. Disinfect pruners in 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP). Remove infected plants immediately.
No direct biological cure. Use cross-protection with mild attenuated virus strains where commercially authorized.

Chemical pesticides are completely ineffective against viruses. Direct chemical sprays towards vector management if insects present. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Plant certified virus-free seed or resistant cultivars (carrying Tm-2^2 gene). Avoid tobacco product use near tomato crops.
Disinfect tools with non-corrosive sterilizers; follow standard worker safety guidelines.
Tomato_Septoria_Leaf_Spot is caused by Septoria lycopersici. Common names: Septoria Leaf Spot (en), سپٹوریا پتے کا دھبہ (ur), د سپټوریا پاڼې ټاپي (ps). Highly destructive foliar fungal disease.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Numerous small circular spots (1–3 mm) with dark brown margins and tan-to-gray centers containing tiny black specks (pycnidia). Lower leaves yellow and drop prematurely.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Practice a 3-year crop rotation. Mulch around base of plants with straw or plastic film to eliminate rain splash from soil. Stake and prune plants.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Remove infected crop debris, destroy nightshade weeds, avoid working in wet fields, and maintain wide row spacing.

metadata.source_name: Cornell University Extension Vegetable MD Online

text: Wear chemical-resistant gloves, eye protection, and protective coveralls during fungicide spraying.

text: Tomato_Spider_Mites is caused by Two-Spotted Spider Mite (Tetranychus urticae). Common names: Spider Mite (en), ٹماٹر کی مکڑی (ur), د ټماټرو د مکوړو طوفان (ps). Arachnid pest sucking plant cell contents.
Fine yellow or white stippling/speckling on upper leaf surfaces. Webbing visible on underside of leaves and growing tips under high infestation. Leaves turn bronze, dry up, and drop.
Favored by hot, dry, dusty weather (> 30°C and low relative humidity). Mites reproduce rapidly under hot drought conditions.
Overhead water misting to increase canopy humidity. Keep field borders and farm roads moist to reduce dust accumulation.
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus). Apply insecticidal soap or horticultural mineral oil.

Apply selective acaricides such as Abamectin, Spiromesifen, or Bifenazate. Note: Broad-spectrum insecticides kill natural predators and worsen outbreaks. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Regular scouting with a 10x hand lens, dust control on access roads, and preserving natural predatory fauna.
Wear protective goggles, gloves, and chemical mask when applying acaricides.
Tomato_Target_Spot is caused by Corynespora cassiicola. Common names: Target Spot (en), ٹماٹر کا ہدف دھبہ (ur), د ټماټرو د هدف ټاپي (ps). Foliar and fruit fungal pathogen.
Small necrotic spots on leaves expanding into brown circular lesions with subtle zonate rings. Fruit lesions are brown, sunken, and crater-like.
Favored by warm humid conditions (20–28°C) and prolonged leaf wetness. Spores are wind-dispersed.
Improve canopy ventilation through wider spacing and trellising. Prune lower diseased foliage and crop residues after harvest.
Foliar sprays of Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Trichoderma species.

Apply protectant Chlorothalonil or systemic strobilurins/triazoles (Azoxystrobin / Difenoconazole). Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Ensure good field drainage, crop rotation, and destruction of alternate host weeds.
Wear chemical gloves, protective clothing, and face shield when handling fungicides.
Tomato_Verticillium_Wilt is caused by Verticillium dahliae. Common names: Verticillium Wilt (en), ورٹیسیلیم مرجھاؤ (ur), د ورټیسیلیوم مړاوی (ps). Soil-borne vascular fungal disease.
V-shaped yellow chlorotic wedges at leaf margins on lower leaves, later turning brown and necrotic. Vascular brown discoloration inside stem base near soil line.
Favored by cool to moderate soil temperatures (20–24°C). Microsclerotia survive in soil for over a decade and infect via root entry points.
Use resistant tomato cultivars (bearing Ve gene). Solarize soil during hot summer months. Rotate with non-susceptible monocot crops (corn, wheat).
Soil application of bio-fungicides containing Trichoderma harzianum or Streptomyces lydicus.
Fumigation or bio-fumigation prior to planting. Drench with Benomyl/Carbendazim derivative. Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Plant certified resistant stock, solarize beds with clear plastic, and avoid transferring infested field soil.
Wear protective gear during soil treatment and handling bio-fumigants.
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus is caused by TYLCV (Begomovirus). Common names: Yellow Leaf Curl (en), ٹماٹر کا پیلا پتا موڑ وائرس (ur), د ټماټرو ژیړ پاڼې قاش وائرس (ps). Whitefly-transmitted virus.
Severe plant stunting, erect bushy growth habit, upward curling of leaf margins, interveinal chlorosis (yellowing), and complete flower abortion leading to zero fruit yield.
Exclusively transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). High whitefly populations lead to 100% crop loss in young fields.
Install yellow sticky traps for whitefly monitoring. Cover seedbeds with 50-mesh insect-proof netting. Rogue out infected plants within 3 weeks of transplanting.
Release whitefly natural enemies (Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus). Apply Neem oil or Beauveria bassiana.

Control whitefly vector using systemic insecticides (Imidacloprid, Acetamiprid, or Spirotetramat). Note: Direct virucides do not exist. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Plant TYLCV-resistant hybrid varieties (Ty-1/Ty-3 genes), use 50-mesh netting, and clear weed hosts (Abutilon, Solanum nigrum).
Wear chemical-resistant gloves, protective clothing, and respirator during vector spray operations.
Potato_Early_Blight is caused by Alternaria solani. Common names: Potato Early Blight (en), آلو کا اگیتا جھلساؤ (ur), د کچالو دمخه سوځیدنه (ps). Important foliar disease of potato.
Dark brown, dry, circular spots with concentric target-ring patterns bordered by yellow leaf margins. Tuber lesions are dark, brown, circular, and dry-rotted.
Favored by alternating wet and dry weather, warm temperatures (24–30°C), and nutrient-stressed plants. Airborne spores spread by wind and rain.
Maintain adequate nitrogen and potassium fertilization. Practice 3-year crop rotation. Irrigate in early morning to allow canopy drying.
Foliar applications of Trichoderma species or Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide formulations.
Apply Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, or Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole premix. Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Use high-quality certified seed tubers, maintain vine nutrition, destroy haulms prior to harvest, and avoid tuber mechanical damage.
Wear protective gloves, eye goggles, and coveralls when applying fungicides.
Potato_Late_Blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans. Common names: Potato Late Blight (en), آلو کا پچھیتا جھلساؤ (ur), د کچالو وروسته سوځیدنه (ps). Most destructive potato disease globally.
Water-soaked dark lesions on leaves and stems that expand rapidly. White mildew growth on leaf undersides in humid weather. Tubers show reddish-brown dry rot extending into flesh.
Favored by cool, wet weather (15–20°C, RH > 90%). Sporangia are windborne and wash down into soil infecting tubers.
Hill soil high around potato vines to protect tubers from sporangia splash. Destroy infected vines (haulm destruction) 2 weeks before harvest.
Apply copper octanoate or bio-control preparations (Bacillus subtilis) prior to high-risk weather windows.
Apply systemic and contact fungicides (Metalaxyl + Mancozeb, Cymoxanil, or Fluazinam). Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Plant certified blight-free seed tubers, use resistant varieties, eliminate cull piles, and monitor forecasting models.
Wear chemical-resistant suit, neoprene gloves, and respirator when spraying late blight fungicides.
Potato_Healthy represents healthy Solanum tuberosum foliage. Common names: Healthy Potato (en), صحت مند آلو (ur), روغ کچالو (ps). Clean foliage free from foliar or vascular damage.
Leaves show vibrant green color, uniform compound leaf canopy, smooth petioles, and zero dark spots, wilting, or stunting.
Maintained through cool-to-moderate climate (15–25°C), adequate soil moisture, well-drained fertile loam, and balanced nutrition.
Perform regular earthing-up (hilling), maintain scheduled drip/furrow irrigation, and apply balanced N-P-K fertilizer.
Soil enrichment with bio-fertilizers (Azotobacter, PSB) and Trichoderma root inoculants.
No chemical intervention needed. Monitor routinely for early pest or disease incursions.
Plant clean seed, maintain weed-free fields, practice proper crop rotation, and avoid waterlogging.
Follow safe agricultural field management guidelines.

Potato_Bacterial_Soft_Rot is caused by Pectobacterium carotovorum or Dickeya species. Common names: Soft Rot / Blackleg (en), آلو کا نرم سڑاند (ur), د کچالو نرم پوسیدګي (ps). Bacterial tuber and stem rot.
Water-soaked mushy tuber rot with foul odor. In field, black slimy decay of lower stems (blackleg symptom), causing plant wilting and stunting.
Favored by waterlogged soil, high temperatures (> 25°C), and tuber wounds. Spreads via handling equipment, wash water, and insects.
Plant seed tubers intact (avoid cutting seed). Ensure well-drained soils. Dry tubers thoroughly before storage and maintain cold ventilated storage (4–6°C).
Apply copper-based seed treatments or bio-bactericides containing Bacillus subtilis prior to storage.
No effective curative chemical bactericide available. Copper Hydroxide soil drench offers minor protection. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Use certified disease-free seed, sanitize storage bins and potato machinery, avoid harvesting wet soils, and handle tubers gently.
Wear protective gloves and mask when applying sanitizing agents to storage facilities.
Potato_Viral_Leaf_Roll is caused by Potato leafroll virus (PLRV). Common names: Potato Leafroll Virus (en), آلو کا پتا موڑ وائرس (ur), د کچالو پاڼې تاوېدو وائرس (ps). Aphid-transmitted luteovirus.
Upward rolling of leaf margins starting on lower leaves (primary infection) or upper leaves (secondary infection). Leaves become thick, leathery, and brittle. Net necrosis inside tubers.
Transmitted in a persistent manner by green peach aphids (Myzus persicae). Systemically infects tubers, perpetuating through seed generations.
Rogue out infected plants and destroy seed tubers. Use virus-tested nuclear seed stock. Destroy aphid host weeds near potato fields.
Conserve natural aphid predators (ladybird beetles, lacewings, parasitoid wasps). Apply Neem oil or insecticidal soap.

Apply systemic aphicides (Imidacloprid, Thiamethoxam, or Flonicamid) to control aphid vector. Note: Direct virucides do not exist. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Plant certified virus-tested seed tubers, manage aphid vectors early, and rogue diseased plants.
Wear chemical-resistant gloves, coveralls, and face shield when applying systemic aphicides.
Potato_Viral_PVX is caused by Potato virus X (PVX). Common names: Potato Virus X / Latent Mosaic (en), آلو کا ایکس وائرس (ur), د کچالو ایکس وائرس (ps). Highly contagious potexvirus.
Faint mild green mosaic mottling on leaves, often latent (symptomless). When co-infected with Potato Virus Y (PVY), causes severe rugose mosaic and plant collapse.
Mechanically transmitted by plant-to-plant contact, machinery, tools, livestock, and infected seed tubers. No insect vector required.
Disinfect tractor tires, cutting knives, and machinery with 10% trisodium phosphate or bleach. Rogue out symptomatic plants.
No biological control agent available for PVX. Maintain high field hygiene.
Chemical pesticides are ineffective against plant viruses. Direct field efforts toward sanitation. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Use certified PVX-free seed tubers, sanitize cutting blades, and avoid mechanical injury during cultivation.
Follow equipment sanitation safety guidelines.
Potato_Viral_PVY is caused by Potato virus Y (PVY). Common names: Potato Virus Y / Rugose Mosaic (en), آلو کا وائی وائرس (ur), د کچالو وای وائرس (ps). Non-persistently aphid-transmitted potyvirus.
Severe mosaic mottling, crinkling/rugosity of leaves, leaf dropping (streak symptom), and Potato Tuber Necrotic Ringspot Disease (PTNRD) on tubers.
Transmitted non-persistently within seconds by numerous aphid species. Also transmitted systemically via infected seed tubers.
Plant PVY-resistant potato varieties. Apply mineral crop oils to leaf canopy to interfere with aphid virus transmission during probing.
Encourage natural aphid predators (Chrysoperla carnea, Coccinella septempunctata).

Apply mineral oil sprays (1–2%) weekly. Systemic insecticides have limited effect on non-persistent transmission but control aphid populations. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Use certified PVY-tested seed, isolation of seed production fields, and early haulm destruction.
Wear protective clothing and goggles when applying agricultural mineral oil sprays.

Pepper_Bacterial_Spot is caused by Xanthomonas euvesicatoria. Common names: Pepper Bacterial Spot (en), شملہ مرچ کا بیکٹیریائی دھبہ (ur), د مرچکو باکتریایي ټاپي (ps). Serious bacterial disease of sweet and hot peppers.

text: Pepper_Cercospora_Leaf_Spot is caused by Cercospora capsici. Common names: Frogeye Leaf Spot (en), فرگ آئی دھبہ (ur), د فرګ آی ټاپي (ps). Fungal leaf spot of pepper.
Circular spots with light gray to white centers and dark reddish-brown margins ('frogeye' appearance) on leaves and stems. Severe infection causes leaf yellowing and defoliation.
Favored by warm temperatures (25–30°C) and high humidity or leaf wetness. Wind and rain splash spread conidia.
Prune lower foliage, space plants properly, avoid overhead sprinklers, and destroy crop residues post-harvest.
Foliar application of Trichoderma harzianum or bio-rational copper compounds.
Apply Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or Azoxystrobin protectant fungicides. Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Crop rotation for 2 years, certified seed, balanced fertilization, and good soil drainage.
Wear protective gloves, mask, and goggles during fungicide spraying.
Pepper_Healthy represents healthy Capsicum annuum foliage. Common names: Healthy Pepper (en), صحت مند شملہ مرچ (ur), روغ مرچک (ps). Disease-free green pepper plant.
Leaves display rich dark green glossy color, smooth intact margins, turgid structure, and freedom from chlorosis, spotting, or insect damage.
Maintained in warm sunny environments (21–28°C), moist well-drained soil, and balanced macro/micronutrient supply.
Maintain drip irrigation, weed control, regular balanced N-P-K fertigation, and staking where necessary.
Incorporate mycorrhizae or beneficial rhizobacteria into soil to support vigor.
No chemical application required. Monitor fields weekly for pests.
Field sanitation, certified seed, proper drainage, and crop rotation.
Follow safe farming and worker protection procedures.
Pepper_Leaf_Curl is caused by Chilli leaf curl virus (ChiLCV). Common names: Chilli Leaf Curl (en), مرچ کا پتا موڑ وائرس (ur), د مرچکو پاڼې قاش وائرس (ps). Whitefly-transmitted begomovirus.
Upward curling and puckering of leaves, vein yellowing, severe leaf size reduction, shortened internodes (stunted bushy appearance), and flower drop.
Transmitted persistently by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). Widespread in tropical and sub-tropical chilli and bell pepper growing regions.
Use 50-mesh insect netting on nurseries. Install yellow sticky traps. Rogue infected plants early. Eradicate weed hosts.
Release predatory mites or lacewings. Apply Neem oil (10,000 ppm) or entomopathogenic fungi (Beauveria bassiana).

Control whitefly vector using systemic insecticides (Imidacloprid, Acetamiprid, or Spirotetramat). Note: Direct virucides do not exist. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Grow resistant cultivars, use 50-mesh nursery nets, and control whitefly populations proactively.
Wear chemical-resistant gloves, suit, and face shield when applying vector insecticides.

Pepper_Nutrition_Deficiency is an abiotic physiological disorder caused by inadequate Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium, Calcium, or Magnesium supply. Common names: Nutrient Deficiency (en), غذائی کیمیائی کمی (ur), د غذایي توکو کمښت (ps).

metadata.source_name: FAO Soil and Plant Nutrition Manual

text: Pepper_Powdery_Mildew is caused by Leveillula taurica (syn. Oidiopsis taurica). Common names: Pepper Powdery Mildew (en), پاؤڈری ملڈیو (ur), د مرچکو سپین خاکستري (ps). Endophytic powdery mildew fungal pathogen.
Bright yellow chlorotic patches on upper leaf surfaces corresponding to white powdery fungal growth on leaf undersides. Severe infection causes extensive leaf drop.
Favored by warm dry climate with high relative humidity (20–35°C, RH > 70%). Unlike most fungi, does not require free water on leaves for infection.
Avoid overcrowding plants. Remove and destroy infected lower leaves. Ensure adequate field ventilation.
Apply bio-rationals such as Potassium Bicarbonate, Sulfur dusting, or Neem oil (1%).
Apply systemic triazole or strobilurin fungicides (Myclobutanil, Penconazole, or Azoxystrobin). Note: Active ingredients only. Registration status: UNVERIFIED -- requires current local label check.
Plant resistant pepper varieties, monitor undersides of leaves, and apply preventive sulfur early.
Wear chemical mask, protective suit, and eye goggles during sulfur or fungicide dusting.
